q-210743:
Let's set $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3x}\cdot 3\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}}{x}\,\text{d}x & =9\int \sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =9\int \sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =9\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =9\cdot \frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}+C \\  & =6{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =6\sqrt{{ln}^{3}⁡(3x)}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-2194:
Let's set $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{2}}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\sqrt{2}\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{ln}⁡x|+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

q-31394:
Let $u={log}_{5}⁡x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,⟹\,\operatorname{ln}⁡5\,\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{5}⁡x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {log}_{5}⁡x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =\int u\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡5\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡5\int u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡5\cdot \frac{{u}^{2}}{2}+C \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡5\cdot \frac{{log}_{5}^{2}⁡x}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-210751:
Let $u={log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3}).$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,⟹\,\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{3}\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})}{2x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int {log}_{5}⁡({x}^{3})\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int u\cdot (\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{6}\int u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{6}\cdot \frac{{u}^{2}}{2}+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5{log}_{5}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})}{12}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-31619:
Let's set $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x).$ Then  we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5x}\cdot 5=\frac{1}{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives the following:

| $x$ | $e/5$ | ${e}^{4}/5$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

We now substitute and evaluate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{e/5}^{{e}^{4}/5}\frac{3}{x\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)}}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{e/5}^{{e}^{4}/5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡(5x)}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3{\int }_{1}^{4}{u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot {\frac{{u}^{1/2}}{1/2}|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =6\cdot {\sqrt{u}|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =6(\sqrt{4}-\sqrt{1}) \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

q-73657:
Let $u={log}_{8}⁡(2x).$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2x\operatorname{ln}⁡8}\cdot 2=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡8}\,⟹\,\operatorname{ln}⁡8\,\text{d}u=\frac{\text{d}x}{x}.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives the following:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1/3$ | $2/3$ |

We now substitute and evaluate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{6{log}_{8}⁡(2x)}{x}\,\text{d}x & =6{\int }_{1}^{2}{log}_{8}⁡(2x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{x} \\  & =6{\int }_{1/3}^{2/3}u\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡8\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡8{\int }_{1/3}^{2/3}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\operatorname{ln}⁡8\cdot \frac{{u}^{2}}{2}{|}_{1/3}^{2/3} \\  & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡8\cdot (\frac{4}{9}-\frac{1}{9}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡8\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
{(x,y)\in {Z}^{2}\,:\,-1\le x\le 2,\,-2\le y\le 3}

The points in our set include all those that lie *above* the line $y=-1.$ For those points, the following condition is satisfied:

$$

q-181690:
The points in our set include all those that lie *above* the line $y=-2$ and *below* the line $y=2.$

A point $P(x,y)$ lies *inside* the shaded region if the following conditions are satisfied:

$$
y>-2,\,y<2.
$$

Combining this into a single condition, we have

$$
-2<y<2.
$$

We must also include the line $y=2$ since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the corresponding inequality symbol above as follows:

$$
-2<y\le 2
$$

Moreover, since we're considering *every* real value in this region, $x\in R,y\in R,$ and therefore 

$$
(x,y)\in R\times R={R}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,-2<y\le 2}.
$$

q-181600:

A point $P(x,y)$ lies *inside* the shaded region if the following conditions are satisfied:

$$
y>-x,\,y<2.
$$

Combining this into a single condition, we have

$$
-x<y<2.
$$

We must also include the line $y=-x$ since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the corresponding inequality symbol above as follows:

$$
-x\le y<2
$$

Moreover, since we're considering *every* real value in this region, $x\in R,y\in R,$ and therefore 

$$
(x,y)\in R\times R={R}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as

{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,-x\le y<2}.
$$

q-181172:
The points in our set include all those that lie *below* the curve $y={x}^{2}.$

Therefore, a point $P(x,y)$ lies *inside* the shaded region if the following condition is satisfied:

$$
y<{x}^{2}
$$

We must also include the curve $y={x}^{2}$ since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the inequality symbol above as follows:

$$
y\le {x}^{2}
$$

Moreover, since we're considering *every* real value in this region, $x\in R,y\in R,$ and therefore 

$$
(x,y)\in R\times R={R}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y\le {x}^{2}}.
$$

q-4782:
We start by integrating the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $x(0)=3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(0))+C \\ 3 & =-\frac{1}{2}+C \\ C & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is

$$
x(t)=\frac{7}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

q-102998:
We start by integrating the acceleration to get the velocity $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (6t+9{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=6.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =3(1)^{2}+3(1)^{3}+C \\ 6 & =6+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is given by $v(t)=3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3}.$ 

Now, we integrate the velocity to get $x(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}+3{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}+\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4}+K\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $K$, we use the fact that $x(1)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =(1)^{3}+\frac{3}{4}(1)^{4}+K \\ 2 & =\frac{7}{4}+K \\ K & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the position $x$ of the particle at time $t$ is 

$$
x(t)={t}^{3}+\frac{3}{4}{t}^{4}+\frac{1}{4}.
$$

q-98753:
We can classify the equilibrium solutions of an autonomous ODE ${y}^{′}=f(y)$ by examining its phase line.

- An equilibrium solution is a *sink* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *toward* the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *source* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line both point *away* from the equilibrium solution.

- An equilibrium solution is a *node* if the arrows directly above and below it on the phase line point in the same direction.

The phase line that corresponds to the given graph is as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14096422/assets/7ad82b4ff48bbf69efccf5a822c7013929224a1a6e6e63e1948ea9ea95dcc858.png)

Therefore, we have:

- Statement I is false while statement II is true. From the phase line, we see that $y=2$ is a source.

- Statement III is true. From the phase line, we see that $y=-4$ is a sink.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only".
